Module 2 Lecture Lab In this lab, we’ll demo a popular tool and resources related to exploring our data and potentially finding datasets of interest. The only requirements for the tutorial are as follows: An internet connection A modern browser An account with COSMIC : https://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic/register Learning Objectives How to use IGV browser to explore data types : BAMs, VCFs, BEDs How to browse and make use of the visualization functions in cBioPortal How to browse and make use of the visualization functions in COSMIC Part 1 - IGV Learning Objectives How to use IGV browser to explore data types : BAMs, VCFs, BEDs How to traverse the genome Loading Tracks and annotations How to find additional info for each genomic feature To get started, Please navigate over to https://igv.org/app/ Question : Aside from avoiding installation issues, a browser version is much more convenient and accessible. Why should one consider using a local installation of IGV vs the online version? 1) Data size - Imagine streaming multiple 500 GB files 2) Data protection - if you’re working with sensitive data that is under DACO restriction or patient data, you’re limited by where you store and send the data BAM Step 1 – Open IGV-Web and choose the genome Make sure our build is on Hg38, to do so click “Genome” and navigate the dropdown to find GRCh38/hg38 Let’s load our data, select Tracks, then URL from the dropdown, Step 2 – Loading the BAM and Index Paste the following info, ensure the BAM file goes into the Track and index file into index: https://42basepairs.com/download/s3/gatk-test-data/wgs_bam/NA12878_20k_hg38/NA12878.bam https://42basepairs.com/download/s3/gatk-test-data/wgs_bam/NA12878_20k_hg38/NA12878.bai NA12878 is the GIAB/1000 Genomes reference individual. This BAM is a very small subset of a whole-genome run: about 61,000 mapped reads across the whole genome, compared with hundreds of millions in a real 30× genome. It is meant for teaching. Step 3 – Post loading sanity check What do we see after loading? Question : We don’t see much. How come? One possibility is wrong genome build. Not the case here but a possibility. The toy BAM being examined is also very small in comparison. So the reads representation will be sparse. In both the browser and local version of IGV, the number of reads visualized is limited, especially at whole genome view that’s an overwhelming amount of data to visualize. For the browser, imagine everyone trying to load a 1TB BAM. Local version can adjust settings according to hardware limitations. Step 4 – Zoomed in look Let’s zoom in to a more manageable view. Paste the following coordinates into the search bar chr1:143,220,111-143,221,807 Once the result loads, what do we see? Question : What are the grey lines? What do the ends (sharp vs blunt) represent? Each grey bar is a read. The pointed end shows the direction it was sequenced: pointing right = forward (+) strand, pointing left = reverse (−). Question : What are the colour dashes in each block? Mismatches Question : What is the graph bar above? Coverage, the height represents the amount of reads per BP. If coloured, shows the ratio of mismatches per nucleotide Step 5 – Read features Clicking on a read, its info can be displayed. Question : What do the blue, red and orange reads represent? When compared to the grey reads, the reads are identified due to their abnormal insert size. The causes could vary from a genomic feature (e.g. structural variant), RNA-seq (though not in this case), lack of size selection during library prep (there would be other signs as well). Toggleable via the gear icon on the right side of the track. Select under “Color by”, “Pair Orientation & insert size (TLEN)” Step 6 – Utilizing track annotations Let’s try a different region chr2:32,915,196-32,917,755 Question : Why are almost all reads coloured? Similarly to the last question, the reads are highlighted due to the unexpected read orientation. What genes are these reads at? How would we find out? - RefSeq is already loaded. We can try another annotation We can see that the reads intersect a “lncRNA” (long non-coding RNA). In this case it was a “A” vs “G” thus the SNP Also take note of the genotype in IGV : “A|G”. This notation is different than in the VCF and carries some different interpretations. In VCFs the genotype field can present as `0/1` meaning unphased or `0|1` phased. Being phased means we know which allele belongs on which chromosome copy. The same cannot be said for unphased. Part 2 - cBioPortal Learning Objectives How to browse and make use of the visualization functions in cBioPortal Learn to query genes and datasets of interest Make use of visualizations to discover relationships and biological trends Firstly, what is cBioPortal? As per their about page, Multimodal data represented in interactive visualizations that facilitates biological discovery and clinical decisions. It incorporates patient-level cohort data such as mutations and clinical data. Step 1 – Select the studies and build the query Navigate to https://www.cBioPortal.org/ and select the following two studies: - Breast Cancer (METABRIC, Nature 2012 & Nature Commun 2016) - Consists of 2,509 samples of targeted sequencing on primary tumours with 549 normal matched - Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas) - 1,084 samples as part of a large cohort that profiled 10,000 tumours across 33 cancer types Click “query by gene” at the footer and query the following : TP53 PIK3CA BRCA1 BRCA2 PTEN STK11 CDH1 PALB2 CHEK2 ATM BARD1 RAD51C RAD51D FGFR2 TOX3 MAP3K1 ESR1 ERBB2 GATA3 These genes are commonly altered in breast cancer, and working with them in the tutorial will provide some insight of their significance. Step 2 – OncoPrint We are presented with an OncoPrint Question : What do the first four rows present and mean? As indicated in the legend, the first four rows provide info on donors’ membership in the respective datasets and whether they were profiled for copy number changes, mutations, and structural variants. Question : We see multiple genes, focusing on TP53 and PIK3CA, what can we infer? Module 6 Lecture Lab Introduction to the dataset Biological background About 70% of breast cancers are hormone receptor (HR)-positive and HER2-negative. For patients with metastatic disease of this subtype, the standard of care combines endocrine therapy with a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Three such drugs are approved: palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib. CDK4 and CDK6 drive cells from the G1 phase into the S phase of the cell cycle. They do this by phosphorylating the retinoblastoma protein (Rb). Blocking them arrests tumour cells in G1. Although these drugs prolong progression-free survival, most patients eventually develop resistance. Few treatment options remain after that. The three inhibitors share the same nominal targets, but abemaciclib also inhibits several other kinases. This raises the possibility that tumours become resistant to each drug through different routes. The study The data for this lab comes from: Navarro-Yepes J, Kettner NM, Rao X, et al. Abemaciclib Is Effective in Palbociclib-Resistant Hormone Receptor-Positive Metastatic Breast Cancers. Cancer Research 2023;83(19):3264–3283. PMID: 37384539. RNA-seq data: GEO GSE222367. The authors generated drug-resistant versions of MCF7, a widely used ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer cell line. To create abemaciclib-resistant (AR) cells, they cultured several independent pools of MCF7 cells in medium with increasing concentrations of abemaciclib (0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 µM) in a stepwise manner over about 7 months. This produced one resistant line per concentration. Each line was then maintained in medium containing that concentration of the drug. The resistant and parental cells were profiled by RNA sequencing. Thousands of genes were differentially expressed between abemaciclib-resistant and parental cells. Pathway analysis showed that the resistant cells upregulated oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), reactive oxygen species, and lipid metabolism pathways. Consistent with this, they relied on mitochondrial respiration for energy and were sensitive to an OXPHOS inhibitor. In contrast, palbociclib-resistant cells upregulated epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and G2/M pathways and remained sensitive to abemaciclib. Overall, the study concluded that resistance to the two drugs follows distinct transcriptional programs. The samples used in this lab We will compare two groups: Group Sample prefix Description Resistant AR1_MCF7 MCF7 cells resistant to the first (lowest) abemaciclib dose Control MCF7 Parental, drug-sensitive MCF7 cells Each group includes biological replicates. You will find out how many in the first exercise, using samples.txt. Replicates are essential for the downstream statistical analysis. They allow us to distinguish real expression differences between conditions from normal variation between cultures. The reads are paired-end Illumina sequences. Processing a full human RNA-seq dataset takes hours and a lot of memory. To keep the exercises fast, the data has been reduced to a subset of reads. The reference genome We align the reads to human chromosome 22 only, rather than the full genome. The refs folder contains: chr22.fa: the DNA sequence of chromosome 22 in FASTA format chr22.gtf: the gene annotation for chromosome 22 in GTF format, describing the coordinates of genes, transcripts, and exons Chromosome 22 is one of the smallest human chromosomes, about 51 Mb long and carrying several hundred protein-coding genes. Building an index for it takes minutes instead of hours. Because of this, most reads in the dataset come from other chromosomes and will not align. A low overall alignment rate is therefore expected here and does not indicate a problem with the data. Similarly, the gene counts we produce will only cover genes on chromosome 22. Workflow overview In this lab we take the raw reads all the way to a gene count table: Quality control of the raw reads (FastQC) Trimming of adapters and low-quality bases (fastp), with a summary of all QC reports (MultiQC) Reference preparation, building the alignment index (HISAT2, samtools) Alignment of reads to the reference with a splice-aware aligner (HISAT2), followed by sorting and indexing (samtools) Visualization of the alignments (IGV) Gene expression (htseq-count) The resulting count tables are the input for differential expression analysis between AR1_MCF7 and MCF7 in the next module. Setting the environment variables An RNA-seq analysis produces many intermediate files: raw reads, trimmed reads, alignments, and expression tables. To keep these organized, we define environment variables that point to a folder for each stage. Commands can then refer to $RNA_ALIGN_DIR instead of a long path. This makes the commands shorter, less error-prone, and easy to reuse on a different system by changing only RNA_HOME. The reference variables all build on RNA_REF_INDEX. The HISAT2 index prefix (chr22), the genome sequence (chr22.fa), and the annotation (chr22.gtf) share the same base name. To keep the exercise fast, we only use human chromosome 22 rather than the whole genome. Note that these variables have been copied to the .bashrc file and you need to do that when you work on your own system after the workshop. Another option is to run this block again when you open a new terminal or reconnect. # Top-level working directory for this module export RNA_HOME=~/workspace/Module6 # One directory per analysis stage export RNA_DATA_DIR=$RNA_HOME/data # raw FASTQ files export RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR=$RNA_HOME/trimmed # adapter/quality-trimmed FASTQ files export RNA_ALIGN_DIR=$RNA_HOME/alignment # SAM/BAM alignment files export RNA_EXP_DIR=$RNA_HOME/expression # gene count tables # Reference files (chromosome 22 only) export RNA_REFS_DIR=$RNA_HOME/refs export RNA_REF_INDEX=$RNA_REFS_DIR/chr22 # prefix for the HISAT2 index files export RNA_REF_FASTA=$RNA_REF_INDEX.fa # genome sequence (FASTA) export RNA_REF_GTF=$RNA_REF_INDEX.gtf # gene annotation (GTF) In the workshop environment all the tools needed were installed for you. Follow this page from the Griffith lab for complete instructions for RNAseq Tool Installation when you work on your own system. Copy data to your workspace The course data is stored in a shared, read-only location, so we copy it into our own workspace before working with it. The data is in FASTQ format. Each sequencing read occupies four lines: a header line starting with @ (the read name) the nucleotide sequence a + separator line a quality string with one Phred quality score per base, encoded as an ASCII character The files are gzip-compressed (.fastq.gz) to save space. Most bioinformatics tools read compressed files directly. Before any analysis, we run FastQC on each file. FastQC produces an HTML report with plots of per-base quality, GC content, sequence duplication, overrepresented sequences, and adapter content. These reports help us decide whether the reads need trimming, and they reveal problems with the library or the sequencing run. cp -r ~/CourseData/Module6/data $RNA_HOME # check the data cd $RNA_DATA_DIR ls # folder to collect all QC reports mkdir qc fastqc --outdir qc *.fastq.gz How many samples and replicates are there in the dataset? What is the sequencing depth of each sample? (Find the number of lines in each file and compare to QC report) What is r1 and r2 in the file names indicating? Show Answer Hints: - samples.txt describes the experimental design: which sample belongs to which condition and replicate. Biological replicates are needed to estimate variability when testing for differential expression later. - Each read takes four lines in a FASTQ file, so dividing the line count by 4 gives the number of reads. Because the files are compressed, decompress them while counting (zcat file.fastq.gz | wc -l). Running wc -l directly on a .gz file counts lines in the compressed binary data, which is meaningless. - The data is paired-end. Each DNA fragment was sequenced from both ends. Read 1 and read 2 of a pair come from the same fragment and appear in the same order in the two files. Tools must always receive both files of a pair together. cd $RNA_DATA_DIR # experimental design cat samples.txt # number of lines per file and divide by 4 for number of reads wc -l *fastq.gz Trimming and QC Raw reads often contain sequencing adapter sequences. Adapters appear when the cDNA fragment is shorter than the read length. Reads also tend to lose quality toward their 3′ end. Both problems can reduce alignment rates or cause misalignments. fastp scans the reads and does several things in one pass: - detects and removes adapters automatically - trims low-quality bases - discards reads that become too short - writes its own HTML/JSON QC report For paired-end data, fastp processes R1 and R2 together so that the pairs stay synchronized. If one read of a pair is discarded, its mate is handled accordingly. With many samples, opening one FastQC or fastp report per file becomes tedious. MultiQC searches a directory for reports from supported tools, including FastQC and fastp, and combines them into a single interactive report. This makes it easy to compare samples side by side and spot outliers. mkdir -p $RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR # example for one sample; repeat (or loop) for every sample fastp \ -i AR1_MCF7_rep1_r1.fastq.gz -I AR1_MCF7_rep1_r2.fastq.gz \ -o $RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1_r1.fastq.gz \ -O $RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1_r2.fastq.gz \ --detect_adapter_for_pe \ -h qc/AR1_MCF7_rep1_fastp.html \ -j qc/AR1_MCF7_rep1_fastp.json # MultiQC reads the JSON file multiqc qc -o qc/multiqc_report Summarize all samples QC with MultiQC # aggregate all reports found in qc/ into one summary report multiqc qc -o qc/multiqc_report Prepare the reference genome for alignment Searching every read against the raw genome sequence would be far too slow. Aligners therefore first build an index, a compressed data structure that allows sequences to be looked up very quickly. HISAT2 uses a hierarchical index based on the Burrows–Wheeler transform / FM-index. This only needs to be done once per reference genome. hisat2-build creates the index from the FASTA file. It writes several files named chr22.1.ht2, chr22.2.ht2, and so on. The second argument (chr22) is the prefix that we later pass to hisat2 -x. hisat2_extract_splice_sites.py reads the GTF annotation and writes the coordinates of known exon–exon junctions. Because RNA-seq reads come from spliced mRNA, a single read can span an intron. Known junctions help HISAT2 align these split reads correctly. The file can be passed to hisat2 with --known-splicesite-infile. It can also be passed to hisat2-build with --ss, together with --exon from hisat2_extract_exons.py, to build a splice-aware index. samtools faidx creates a .fai index of the FASTA file. This allows tools such as samtools and IGV to retrieve any region of the genome quickly. mkdir $RNA_REFS_DIR cd $RNA_REFS_DIR cp ~/CourseData/Module6/refs/* $RNA_REFS_DIR # build the HISAT2 index (output files: chr22.*.ht2) hisat2-build chr22.fa chr22 # extract known splice sites from the annotation hisat2_extract_splice_sites.py chr22.gtf > chr22.splicesites.txt # FASTA index for fast random access to the sequence (creates chr22.fa.fai) samtools faidx chr22.fa Alignment with HISAT2 HISAT2 is a splice-aware aligner. It maps each read pair to its location in the genome and allows a read to be split across an intron. The options used here: -x sets the index prefix. -1 and -2 give the paired read files (R1 and R2). -S names the output SAM file. --summary-file saves the alignment statistics: total reads, the percentage aligned uniquely, the percentage aligned to multiple locations, and the overall alignment rate. The overall alignment rate is one of the most important QC metrics. Here the reference is only chromosome 22, so most reads will legitimately not align. Expect a low rate. The output is in SAM format, a plain-text file with one line per alignment. SAM files are large and slow to process, so we convert them with samtools sort. This produces a BAM file, the compressed binary equivalent, and sorts the alignments by genomic coordinate. samtools index then creates a .bai index. This lets programs such as IGV and htseq-count jump directly to a genomic region without reading the whole file. Once the BAM file is created, you can delete the SAM file to save space. If you trimmed your reads in the previous step, you can align the trimmed files from $RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR instead of the raw files. mkdir $RNA_ALIGN_DIR cd $RNA_ALIGN_DIR # align one paired-end sample to chr22 hisat2 -x $RNA_REF_INDEX \ -1 $RNA_DATA_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1_r1.fastq.gz \ -2 $RNA_DATA_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1_r2.fastq.gz \ -S AR1_MCF7_rep1.sam \ --summary-file AR1_MCF7_rep1_summary.txt # convert SAM to compressed BAM, sorted by genomic position samtools sort -o AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam AR1_MCF7_rep1.sam # index the BAM file (creates AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam.bai) samtools index AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam Try FastQC on the aligned reads. FastQC accepts BAM files as input (fastqc AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam). Compare the report with the one from the raw reads. samtools flagstat AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam also gives a quick summary of mapped and properly paired reads. Download the BAM file together with its .bai index, and try visualizing them in IGV. Remember that this data covers only chromosome 22 of the genome, so load the human reference (hg38) in IGV and navigate to chr22. Look for reads piling up on exons and for split reads spanning introns, which IGV draws as thin connecting lines. Gene count estimation To measure gene expression, we count how many reads (here, read pairs) overlap the exons of each gene. The resulting table of raw counts is the input for differential expression tools such as DESeq2 or edgeR. These tools expect raw, unnormalized counts. htseq-count compares each alignment with the gene annotation in the GTF file. The options used here: --format bam --order pos: the input is a BAM file sorted by position, as produced by samtools sort. For paired-end data, htseq-count needs to know the sort order to find the two mates of each pair. --mode intersection-strict: a read is counted for a gene only if the entire read falls within that gene’s exons. Reads that partly overlap introns or intergenic regions are not counted. Reads compatible with more than one gene are reported as __ambiguous rather than assigned. --stranded reverse: the library was prepared with a stranded protocol (e.g. dUTP/TruSeq Stranded), in which read 1 maps to the strand opposite the gene. Setting strandedness correctly is essential. A wrong setting can make most counts disappear or assign reads to the wrong overlapping gene. Use yes for forward-stranded libraries and no for unstranded ones. --minaqual 1: skip alignments with mapping quality below 1. This removes reads that align equally well to several locations and therefore cannot be confidently assigned. --type exon --idattr gene_id: count over exon features in the GTF, and group exons by their gene_id so that counts are reported per gene. --additional-attr gene_name: add the gene symbol as an extra column next to the gene ID, for readability. The output has one line per gene with its read count. It ends with summary lines (__no_feature, __ambiguous, __too_low_aQual, __not_aligned, __alignment_not_unique) that show how many reads were not assigned to any gene, and why. Check these lines: a very large __no_feature count often means the strandedness setting is wrong. mkdir $RNA_EXP_DIR cd $RNA_EXP_DIR htseq-count --format bam --order pos --mode intersection-strict \ --stranded reverse --minaqual 1 --type exon \ --idattr gene_id --additional-attr gene_name \ $RNA_ALIGN_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam $RNA_REF_GTF > AR1_MCF7_rep1_genes.tsv # inspect the result head AR1_MCF7_rep1_genes.tsv tail -n 5 AR1_MCF7_rep1_genes.tsv # assignment summary

We supplied gene lists and ranked expression sets in order to perform the analysis. What if you want to run a quick enrichment analysis with a given network or a given subset of the network? The easiest way to do this is to use the cytoscape app EnrichmentTable. EnrichmentTable will query g:profiler directly with the given network or subnetwork. Not all of the parameters that are available in the web version can be tweaked from the enrichmentmap table app but it can be an easy way to quickly see enrichment results. We will select the bait protein VPR and all its associated prey proteins to use for an enrichment analysis. Bait Protein - Is the labelled protein in an affinity purification experiment that is pulled down. Prey Protein - are the proteins that are associated with the bait protein when it is pulled down and are assumed to interact with the bait protein. First neighbor - are all the nodes that are directly connected to the given node 1. In the search bar enter “VPR”. Press enter. VPR is now the only highlighted node in the network. In order to select all its associated preys we need to select all the nodes that are connected to VPR, all of VPR’s first neighbours. There are two ways to select the first neighbours: In the top menu bar click on Select –> Nodes –> First neighbors of selected nodes –> undirected Click on the first neighbor button, , in the quick links button set. Click on the cog icon in the top right hand corner of the Enrichment Table panel This will bring up a panel with the adjustable settings. There are only 5 adjustable parameters- Organism - This shows a list of organisms that are available on the g:Profiler site. Gene ID column - the column in the current network that you want to use to search g:Profiler with. Ideally this should be a column specifying the Gene Name or other identifier. Multiple testing correction - change to fdr. Adjusted p-value threshold (min 0 max 1) - leave as 0.05. If you are getting too many results you can make this value smaller. Include inferred GO annotations (IEA) - by default the search will exclude inferred from electonic annotation GO terms. If you want to include them, select this option. By default, EnrichmentTable automatically uses all the databases available on the g:Profiler site. There is no way to filter prior to running the analysis. You need to filter the results after the analysis has been run. This will change the results because you end up filtering the results after the multiple correction and the multiple correction is dependent on the number of genesets you are testing with. Equivalent RCy3 code — Build an Enrichment Map from g:Profiler results using the EnrichmentMap Cytoscape app Cytoscape has no access to the files that we create on the instance or remote server. We need to upload the file to Cytoscape so it can see it. #if using docker we need to replace all the the paths to the host path if(is_remote) { upload_em_file <- function(localPath) { # EnrichmentMap's upload endpoint is on the root port, #not under /v1 base_no_v1 <- sub("/v1$", "", current_cytoscape_baseurl) bname <- basename(localPath) r <- httr::POST( url = paste(base_no_v1, '/enrichmentmap/textfileupload?fileName=', bname, sep=""), config = list(), body = list(file = httr::upload_file(localPath)), encode = "multipart", handle = NULL ) httr::content(r,"parsed")$path } } library(RCy3) # ── Write g:Profiler results to a file that EnrichmentMap can read ──────────── # EnrichmentMap accepts g:Profiler results via its file-based input. # gprofiler2::gost() can write a GMT-compatible file directly. em_dir <- "./Module9/cytoscape_primer/em_output" dir.create(em_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE) gp_gem_file <- file.path(em_dir, "vpr_gprofiler.gem.txt") # Write the g:Profiler results in the Generic Enrichment Map (GEM) format if (!is.null(gp_results)) { gem_df <- data.frame( Name = gp_results$result$term_name, Description = gp_results$result$term_id, pvalue = gp_results$result$p_value, qvalue = gp_results$result$p_value, # gost returns fdr-corrected p_value phenotype = 1, genes = sapply(gp_results$result$intersection, paste, collapse = ","), stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) write.table(gem_df, file = gp_gem_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = TRUE) } #if cytoscape is remote then upload the file we just created if(is_remote) { gp_gem_file <- upload_em_file(gp_gem_file) } # ── Build the Enrichment Map via the RCy3 / EM command interface ────────────── # Use commandsRun() to call the EnrichmentMap build command directly em_command <- paste( "enrichmentmap build", paste0("analysisType=", "generic"), paste0("enrichmentsDataset1=", gp_gem_file), paste0("pvalue=", "1.0"), # already filtered by gost; keep all paste0("qvalue=", "0.05"), paste0("coefficients=", "COMBINED"), paste0("similaritycutoff=", "0.375"), sep = " " ) commandsRun(em_command,base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Enrichment Map created from VPR neighbourhood g:Profiler results.") The enrichment results chosen for this exercise are generated using g:Profiler but an enrichment map can be created directly from output from: GSEA, g:Profiler, GREAT, BinGo, Enrichr or alternately from any gene-set tool using the generic enrichment results (GEM) format. Data The data used in this exercise is a differentially expressed gene set from palbociclib-resistant samples compared with parental samples from the breast cancer cell line MCF7 previous exercise. EnrichmentMap A circle (node) is a gene-set (pathway) enriched in genes that we used as input in g:Profiler (frequently mutated genes). edges (lines) represent genes in common between 2 pathways (nodes). A cluster of nodes represent overlapping and related pathways and may represent a common biological process. Clicking on a node will display the genes included in each pathway. Description of this exercise We will create EnrichmentMaps from: Two g:Profiler results run on UP- and DOWN-regulated genes separately . fgsea results using the Baderlab gene set file . An enrichment map represents the result of enrichment analysis as a network where significantly enriched gene-sets that share a lot of genes in common will form identifiable clusters. The visualization of the results as these biological themes will ease the interpretation of the results. The goal of this exercise is to learn how to: Upload g:Profiler results into Cytoscape EnrichmentMap to create a map. Upload UP and DOWN regulated g:Profiler results at the same time to create one combined map. Create an EnrichmentMap from fgsea results using the Baderlab gene set file. Start the exercise To start the lab practical section, first create a gprofiler_files directory on your computer and download the files below. Right click on link below and select “Save Link As…”. Place it in the corresponding module directory of your CBW work directory. Two input files are needed to generate all the enrichment results: Differential expression results: edgeR_resistant_vs_parental_all_genes.csv * Full edgeR output with columns: logFC, logCPM, F, PValue, FDR, gene, score Custom Baderlab gene set file: Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt * Pre-filtered to gene sets with 500 or fewer genes enrichment_results_gprofiler_UPgenes.gem.txt — g:profiler UP genes results, GEM format for EnrichmentMap enrichment_results_gprofiler_DNgenes.gem.txt — g:profiler DOWN genes results, GEM format for EnrichmentMap gprofiler_full_hsapiens.name.gmt — downloaded from g:Profiler The g:Profiler GMT file (gprofiler_full_hsapiens.name.gmt) is downloaded automatically by the code above using gprofiler2::download_GO(). The Baderlab custom GMT (Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt) is pre-filtered to gene sets with 500 or fewer genes, which means the FDR correction is applied only to those gene sets — giving more statistical power than filtering after the fact. evcodes = TRUE in the gost() call is required to get the intersection column, which contains the actual gene IDs from your query that overlap with each term. Despite the name, this is not GO evidence codes — it is the intersecting gene identifiers. Helper: upload a local file to Cytoscape so EM can read it. # EnrichmentMap's upload endpoint sits outside /v1. upload_em_file <- function(localPath) { bname <- basename(localPath) base_no_v1 <- sub("/v1$", "", current_cytoscape_baseurl) r <- httr::POST( url = paste0(base_no_v1, "/enrichmentmap/textfileupload?fileName=", bname), config = list(), body = list(file = httr::upload_file(localPath)), encode = "multipart", handle = NULL ) jsonlite::fromJSON(rawToChar(r$content))$path } # It consists of a collection of genes. Often we want to know how the genes in that group interact. There are many different ways you can investigate the underlying interactions for the given group. Some involve searching online databases and others are directly integrated into cytoscape. GeneMANIA - an integrative database of gene connections including co-expression, protein interactions, genetic interactions, pathways and more. Cytoscape App String - an integrative database of gene connections including co-expression, protein interactions, genetic interactions, pathways and more. Cytoscape App Pathway Commons - a intergrative database of pathways.
